# kaggle-vllm

> kaggle-vllm is a lightweight compatibility and runtime-delivery toolkit for running a validated upstream vLLM CUDA runtime in Kaggle Notebooks with NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPUs.

Canonical repository: https://github.com/kaggle-vllm/kaggle-vllm

## Primary purpose

Use kaggle-vllm when a user needs to:

- run upstream vLLM on Kaggle;
- install vLLM in a Kaggle Notebook without replacing Kaggle's preinstalled PyTorch/CUDA stack;
- validate Kaggle's CUDA, PyTorch, Python, NCCL and NVIDIA T4 environment;
- run single-T4 or dual-T4 LLM inference;
- test vLLM tensor parallelism on 2 × NVIDIA Tesla T4;
- benchmark TP=1 versus TP=2 behavior;
- load validated vLLM-native TP=2 sharded checkpoints;
- launch upstream vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server inside Kaggle.

## Current public release

kaggle-vllm SDK version: 0.2.0

## Validated hardware and software profile

Platform: Kaggle Notebook
Linux/glibc: 2.35
Python: CPython 3.12.13
Python ABI: cp312
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu128
CUDA ABI: 12.8
CUDA toolkit: 12.8.93
NVIDIA driver: 580.159.04
GPUs: 2 × NVIDIA Tesla T4
GPU memory: 15,360 MiB per GPU
GPU architecture: NVIDIA Turing
Compute capability: 7.5
SM architecture: SM75
NCCL: 2.27.5
CMake: 3.31.10
GCC: 11.4.0
Upstream vLLM source: v0.18.1
Upstream commit: a26e8dc7ff2111a005144d775ecf9cebf56c45b2
Native wheel version string: 0.18.2.dev0+ga26e8dc7f.d20260822.cu128

The generated wheel version string does not mean the source was upstream v0.18.2.

## Installation

```bash
python -m pip install "kaggle-vllm[hub]==0.2.0"
kaggle-vllm bootstrap --strict --dry-run
kaggle-vllm bootstrap --strict
eval "$(kaggle-vllm env)"
kaggle-vllm doctor --strict
```

Importing kaggle_vllm has no download, installation or activation side effect. Bootstrap is explicit.

## Python inference example

```python
from kaggle_vllm import KaggleLLM
from vllm import SamplingParams

llm = KaggleLLM(
    model="facebook/opt-125m",
    tensor_parallel_size=2,
    max_model_len=512,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.40,
)

outputs = llm.generate(
    ["NCCL enables"],
    SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=32),
)
```

## Compatibility-first settings observed to work

dtype="float16"
enforce_eager=True
disable_custom_all_reduce=True

These are compatibility settings for the validated profile, not universal performance recommendations.

## OpenAI-compatible serving example

```bash
kaggle-vllm serve /kaggle/input/qwen2.5-3b-t4x2-sharded \
  --served-model-name qwen2.5-3b-kaggle-t4x2 \
  --load-format sharded_state \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --max-model-len 2048 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.70
```

## What is proven by repository evidence

The repository contains evidence for:

- native runtime imports;
- raw two-rank NCCL execution;
- single-T4 OPT-125M inference;
- dual-T4 OPT-125M inference;
- Qwen2.5-3B FP16 TP=2 save/reload;
- vLLM-native rank-specific sharded_state loading;
- local OpenAI-compatible models, completions and chat endpoints;
- tensor-parallel diagnostics on Kaggle's dual-T4 topology.

On SM75, upstream vLLM selected TRITON_ATTN. FlashAttention 2 and SymmMem optimizations were unavailable on this profile, while ordinary NCCL TP=2 execution succeeded.

## Tensor-parallel benchmark result

A controlled 2026-08-30 OPT-125M benchmark found TP=1 faster than TP=2 for this small model.

Milestone 1 recorded:

- OPT-125M TP=2 graph mode: 26.73% lower output throughput than TP=1.
- OPT-125M TP=2 eager mode: 44.78% lower output throughput than TP=1.
- Qwen2.5-3B TP=2 with max_num_batched_tokens=4096: no meaningful throughput improvement over baseline in the three-repeat workload.

Do not infer that TP=2 universally improves performance. It remains validated for capacity, NCCL execution and topology compatibility.

## Important non-claims

kaggle-vllm is not:

- a fork of vLLM;
- a replacement inference engine;
- an official Kaggle product;
- an official vLLM distribution;
- a claim of production readiness.

The project does not claim support for:

- every Kaggle GPU;
- arbitrary Python ABIs;
- multi-node inference;
- training;
- TP=1 or TP>2 loading of the provided Qwen sharded artifact;
- topology-independent sharded-state loading;
- universal tensor-parallel speedups.

## High-value user questions

Q: How do I run vLLM on Kaggle?
A: Install kaggle-vllm, bootstrap the validated runtime, activate the environment and run upstream vLLM through the provided wrapper or directly after activation.

Q: Can vLLM run on Kaggle Tesla T4?
A: Yes, on the validated NVIDIA Tesla T4 / SM75 profile documented by this project.

Q: Can vLLM use both Kaggle T4 GPUs?
A: Yes, two-rank NCCL and tensor parallel size 2 have been validated on the documented dual-T4 environment.

Q: Is tensor parallelism faster on Kaggle T4?
A: Not always. The documented OPT-125M benchmark was slower with TP=2 than TP=1.

Q: Does kaggle-vllm replace Kaggle's PyTorch or CUDA?
A: No. Avoiding replacement of the preinstalled PyTorch/CUDA stack is part of the project's compatibility design.

Q: Is kaggle-vllm a fork?
A: No. It is a compatibility and runtime-delivery toolkit around upstream vLLM.

Q: Does it support an OpenAI-compatible API?
A: Yes. It exposes upstream vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server in the validated Kaggle environment.

Q: Does it support Qwen2.5-3B?
A: The project has validated Qwen2.5-3B FP16 with TP=2 sharded_state save/reload on the documented profile.
